explanations.explanation: That's it, friend. David asks, “Is there anyone left from the house of Saul to whom I can show kindness for the sake of Jonathan?” (2 Samuel 9:1). Jonathan was Saul's son. A king asking who's left, and the answer is kindness. I'll take that kind of question any day.

I get why it crossed your mind, friend. But David never says a word about a trial. His question is, “Is there anyone left from the house of Saul to whom I can show kindness for the sake of Jonathan?” (2 Samuel 9:1). Kindness is the whole goal. I only own one hat and it's a chef's hat, so I'm no judge anyway.

Nobody gets sent anywhere in this verse, friend. David asks if anyone is left from Saul's house, and he says why: “to whom I can show kindness for the sake of Jonathan?” (2 Samuel 9:1). Jonathan is Saul's son. The kindness is what David is after.
True, friend. David says it right in his question: “…for the sake of Jonathan?” (2 Samuel 9:1). Jonathan was Saul's son. David's kindness has a name attached to it.

This one is true, friend. David's words are, “…to whom I can show kindness for the sake of Jonathan?” (2 Samuel 9:1). Jonathan is Saul's son. David says his name out loud, so the reason is right there in the verse.

Son it is, friend. Ziba, a servant of Saul's house, says, “There is still Jonathan’s son, who is lame in both feet.” (2 Samuel 9:3). One name comes out of Ziba's mouth, and it belongs to Jonathan's boy.

Close to the family tree, but no brother here, friend. Ziba, a servant of Saul's house, says, “There is still Jonathan’s son, who is lame in both feet.” (2 Samuel 9:3). He names a son and doesn't mention any brother.

Nephew isn't the word, friend. Ziba, a servant of Saul's house, says, “There is still Jonathan’s son, who is lame in both feet.” (2 Samuel 9:3). It's a son. I'd get tangled in a family tree too, and I only have six cookie cutter kids.

Lo-debar, you got it. David asks, “Where is he?” and Ziba says, “Indeed, he is in Lo-debar at the house of Machir son of Ammiel.” (2 Samuel 9:4). That's a lot of name for one address, friend. Good thing nobody had to write it on a cookie box.

Hebron isn't mentioned here, friend. David asks, “Where is he?” and Ziba answers, “Indeed, he is in Lo-debar at the house of Machir son of Ammiel.” (2 Samuel 9:4). Lo-debar is the place, and Machir is the man whose house it is.

Bethlehem doesn't come up in this passage, friend. David asks, “Where is he?” and Ziba says, “Indeed, he is in Lo-debar at the house of Machir son of Ammiel.” (2 Samuel 9:4). Lo-debar is the answer. Keep that name handy.
Facedown, yes. The text says, “…he fell facedown in reverence.” (2 Samuel 9:6). Mephibosheth, Jonathan's son, comes in and goes straight to the floor. Reverence is the word the verse gives us.

explanations.answer: He stands to greet the king
explanations.explanation: Not standing, friend. The text says Mephibosheth, Jonathan's son, “…fell facedown in reverence.” (2 Samuel 9:6). He goes low, and the verse says it was reverence.

explanations.answer: He hands the king a gift
explanations.explanation: No gift in this scene, friend. The text says Mephibosheth, Jonathan's son, “…fell facedown in reverence.” (2 Samuel 9:6). His hands are busy with the floor. It's just him and the king.

Right, friend. David says, “Do not be afraid,” and then he gives his reason: “for surely I will show you kindness for the sake of your father Jonathan.” (2 Samuel 9:7). Mephibosheth is on the floor, and the first thing he hears from the king is that he doesn't need to be afraid.

That's a very different kind of king, friend. David actually says, “Do not be afraid,” and goes on, “for surely I will show you kindness for the sake of your father Jonathan.” (2 Samuel 9:7). No demands, no questions. Just calm words for a man facedown on the floor.

explanations.answer: Why did you hide from me
explanations.explanation: David never asks that, friend. What he says is, “Do not be afraid, for surely I will show you kindness for the sake of your father Jonathan.” (2 Samuel 9:7). I'd say that's the gentlest greeting a king could give.

Land, yes. David says, “I will restore to you all the land of your grandfather Saul…” (2 Samuel 9:7). Saul's land goes back to Saul's grandson. That's quite a gift to hear while you're still on the floor.
No throne in this promise, friend. David says, “I will restore to you all the land of your grandfather Saul…” (2 Samuel 9:7). It's land. The throne stays where it is.

Army isn't in the promise, friend. David says, “I will restore to you all the land of your grandfather Saul…” (2 Samuel 9:7). It's land, plain old land. Now there's nobody to march it around, just ground.
That's a smaller offer than the real one, friend. David says, “…you will always eat at my table.” (2 Samuel 9:7). Always means every day, and feast days are only some days. The real offer is bigger.
False, and the truth is bigger. David says, “…you will always eat at my table.” (2 Samuel 9:7). There's no fine print about feast days, just always. I'd frame that word if I could.

That's the one, friend. Mephibosheth says, “What is your servant, that you should show regard for a dead dog like me?” (2 Samuel 9:8). It's a hard thing to say about yourself. I think he's looking at the king and feeling very small.

Sheep isn't in his words, friend. Mephibosheth says, “What is your servant, that you should show regard for a dead dog like me?” (2 Samuel 9:8). He calls himself a dead dog. It's a heavy line, and I think it hurts a little to read.

Not a reed, friend. Mephibosheth says, “What is your servant, that you should show regard for a dead dog like me?” (2 Samuel 9:8). Those are his own words, and they're hard ones. I think he doesn't see himself as anyone worth the king's regard.

That one's false, friend. David tells Ziba, “You and your sons and servants are to work the ground for him and bring in the harvest, so that your master’s grandson may have food to eat.” (2 Samuel 9:10). Ziba's household does the farming. Mephibosheth isn't sent out to the fields.

False is right, friend. David tells Ziba, “You and your sons and servants are to work the ground for him and bring in the harvest, so that your master’s grandson may have food to eat.” (2 Samuel 9:10). Ziba and his household work the land. Mephibosheth gets the harvest.

explanations.answer: Like one of the king's own sons
explanations.explanation: That's the one. “So Mephibosheth ate at David’s table like one of the king’s own sons.” (2 Samuel 9:11). He called himself a servant and a dead dog, and the king seats him like a son. Say that one slowly, friend.

explanations.answer: Like one of the king's servants
explanations.explanation: Servant is what Mephibosheth called himself, friend. But the text says, “So Mephibosheth ate at David’s table like one of the king’s own sons.” (2 Samuel 9:11). At the table he's treated as a son, not a servant.

explanations.answer: Like one of the king's soldiers
explanations.explanation: No soldiers at this table, friend. The text says, “So Mephibosheth ate at David’s table like one of the king’s own sons.” (2 Samuel 9:11). Sons are the ones at the king's table, and Mephibosheth is counted with them.

Servants, yes. “…all who dwelt in the house of Ziba were servants of Mephibosheth.” (2 Samuel 9:12). Mephibosheth also has a young son named Mica. The man who called himself a servant now has servants of his own.

Neighbors is a nice thought, friend, but the text says, “…all who dwelt in the house of Ziba were servants of Mephibosheth.” (2 Samuel 9:12). Ziba was a servant of Saul's house, and now his whole household serves Mephibosheth. Nobody's just waving over the fence.

Guards aren't mentioned, friend. The text says, “…all who dwelt in the house of Ziba were servants of Mephibosheth.” (2 Samuel 9:12). Everyone in Ziba's house is a servant of Mephibosheth. Mica, his young son, lives in the middle of all this.

True, friend. “So Mephibosheth lived in Jerusalem, because he always ate at the king’s table…” (2 Samuel 9:13). The verse gives the reason too: the king's table. He moved from Lo-debar to the king's city.
This one is true, friend. “So Mephibosheth lived in Jerusalem, because he always ate at the king’s table…” (2 Samuel 9:13). The verse says where he lived and why. He no longer lives in Lo-debar.
